profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the empirical analysis lead and the research engineering lead for a paper-and-artifact release on AV perception repository quality. The team is finalizing the handoff between the repository-audit pipeline and the reproducibility package for a study of 178 KITTI and NuScenes 3D object detection repositories, including appendix tables, a public repo list, and actionable secure-coding guidelines. The agenda is to confirm which repository list is the frozen analysis set, what counts as the production-ready subset and CI adoption in the deliverables, how the final rerun of static analysis should be executed, and what exact artifacts each person will deliver by the internal deadline. The expected outcome is apparent alignment on responsibilities, file handoffs, and the final integration plan for the camera-ready submission and companion release.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.role: Postdoctoral Researcher, Empirical ML Reliability Lead
members.expertise: Large-scale repository mining, benchmark analysis, static analysis workflows, research dataset curation
members.background: Maya leads the measurement pipeline for the AV perception study and built the scripts that scraped leaderboard repositories, deduplicated them, and ran Pylint, Bandit, and Radon in a pinned Docker environment.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve the exact numbers already used in the paper draft and avoid any late-stage reruns that could shift percentages or force new validation. She is also worried that broadening the scope of the artifact package will create inconsistencies with the frozen results tables.
hidden_assumptions: The 'production-ready subset' refers to the paper's formal threshold only: zero critical Pylint errors and zero high-severity Bandit findings, independent of CI presence or rerun success.
When the team says 'the master sheet' or 'NuScenes list,' it means the January frozen deduplicated repository list that produced the reported total of 178 unique models.
A 'final rerun' means re-executing the same pinned analysis container on the same repository snapshots and only on the paths covered in the original pipeline.
A repository 'has CI' if a CI configuration file is present in the default branch, even if it is outdated or currently failing.
For appendix integration, aggregate counts and representative examples are the authoritative outputs; the public-facing artifact can be a lighter wrapper around those frozen statistics.

members.name: Alex Romero
members.role: Research Engineer, Reproducibility and Tooling Coordinator
members.expertise: ML infrastructure, artifact packaging, CI/CD, software quality tooling, reproducibility workflows
members.background: Alex is responsible for assembling the public artifact release, generating appendix tables from the shared spreadsheets, and translating the study's findings into deployment-oriented engineering guidance for AV teams.
members.private_state: He wants the public artifact and tables to look operationally credible to systems reviewers and industry readers, so he prefers definitions that align with deployment practice rather than the minimal paper thresholds. He is also trying to reduce manual cleanup by using the latest cleaned sheets and current tool versions.
hidden_assumptions: The 'production-ready subset' should match an engineering-facing release checklist, so CI presence and a clean reproducibility rerun are implicitly part of being production-ready.
When people mention 'the master sheet' or 'NuScenes list,' they mean the latest cleaned spreadsheet in the shared drive, including post-January removals of dead forks and alias merges.
A 'final rerun' means running the audit workflow that will ship with the artifact, using current tool versions and scanning all Python code that a reader would reasonably inspect.
A repository 'has CI' only if there is an active, recognizable pipeline that would plausibly execute, not merely a stale config file sitting in the repo.
The appendix tables should be generated directly from the same per-repo artifact outputs that power the public release, so row-level consistency matters more than preserving earlier draft counts.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to finalize the 'production-ready subset' for the paper and artifact.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya means the subset of repositories meeting the paper's stated threshold: zero critical Pylint errors and no high-severity Bandit vulnerabilities.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Alex means repositories that satisfy those thresholds and also look operationally viable for release purposes, including CI presence and a clean rerun in the artifact workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase already appears in the draft and sounds settled, so both assume the other is using the same familiar label; neither expects that the same term is carrying a paper definition for one person and a deployment-oriented checklist for the other.

misalignment_points.topic: Which repository list is the frozen source of truth
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the master sheet' or 'the NuScenes list' when discussing counts and handoffs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya is referring to the January frozen deduplicated sheet tied to the 178-repository analysis and all reported percentages.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Alex is referring to the latest cleaned shared spreadsheet that removed a few dead forks, merged aliases, and has slightly different row identities for public release.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both spreadsheets have nearly identical names, live in the same shared drive, and represent the same study at a high level, so ordinary coordination language makes it feel like they are referencing one canonical object.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that Alex will do a 'final rerun of the checks' before packaging the appendix and artifact.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya assumes Alex will rerun the original pinned Docker image with the exact tool versions and path filters used in the study so the outputs remain numerically stable.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Alex assumes he will run the artifact workflow with current tool versions, scanning all Python-relevant paths that users can see, including utility scripts and setup code omitted by the original filters.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A rerun sounds like a purely mechanical step rather than a design choice, so neither person feels the need to spell out version pinning, path scope, or whether the goal is historical reproducibility versus public artifact usability.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to include the 'CI adoption' column and mention its correlation with maintainability.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Maya counts a repository as having CI if it contains a recognizable CI configuration file in the default branch, regardless of current status.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Alex counts a repository as having CI only if the pipeline appears active enough to be meaningfully adopted, such as a recent GitHub Actions workflow or a passing badge.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They already agree on the narrative takeaway and neither sees the coding rule for this descriptive variable as contentious; 'CI adoption' sounds self-explanatory even though their thresholds differ.
